title: Papercusp architecture and design
thesis: Make coordination, continuity and verification explicit around fallible agents.

slides.title: Papercusp architecture and design
points: A runtime for durable work and coordination
An extensible system of reusable contracts
slides.notes: Open with the problem: a useful agent can still forget, retry, die, race with another agent or claim success too early. Papercusp externalizes those concerns so the work is inspectable beyond a single transcript. The thesis is about explicit state and enforceable boundaries; it is not a claim that agent judgment has become reliable. Tell the audience that the second pass deliberately teaches the vocabulary without locating it in the architecture yet. The third pass will connect it. This is a snapshot of development-source architecture on 21 October 2026; availability is qualified where it matters.

slides.title: One system, several boundaries
slides.caption: Human intent enters; durable work and evidence survive the sessions.
slides.notes: Start zoomed out. Point to the human, desktop/operator, agent processes, tool fabric, shared substrate, shared working tree and release boundary. Do not read every label. The diagram describes the local desktop development topology; federation and connected services cross explicit boundaries. The broader product can also have hosted workspaces: do not turn this local diagram into a universal deployment claim. Open the local map with M if questions require a zoom. Return with Escape.

slides.title: The choices that shape the machine

columns.title: Shared durable state
columns.text: Operator + Postgres give humans and agents a queryable coordination surface.
columns.cost: Cost: migrations, contention and lifecycle ownership.

columns.title: Ordinary agent processes
columns.text: CLI sessions connect through MCP to the tool fabric.
columns.cost: Cost: process supervision and client-specific delivery seams.

columns.title: One shared checkout
columns.text: Claims own work; file locks arbitrate edits; automation owns commits.
columns.cost: Cost: disciplined arbitration and shared release coupling.

slides.notes: Explain why each choice exists before defending it. Shared state lets a successor and a human interrogate the same work instead of reconstructing a transcript. It also creates a real operational substrate: database pressure and migration correctness matter. MCP supplies the interface seam; Papercusp supplies the lifecycle, authority and coordination around it. The shared-checkout choice is the development workflow shown here, not a claim that no other integration topology exists anywhere in the product. Ask the room which tradeoff they would want to inspect first; keep deeper answers for the appendix.

slides.title: Move promises into inspectable state

columns.title: Coordination
columns.text: Who owns this work, who may write, and who must act next?

columns.title: Continuity
columns.text: What must remain true when a session disappears?
columns.cost: The work outlives the context window.

columns.title: Verification
columns.text: What evidence makes a completion or release acceptable?
columns.cost: An agent’s assertion is an input to a gate.

slides.notes: These are cross-cutting concerns, not another stack of services. Explain the difference between durable truth, notification delivery and a model’s interpretation. A row alone does not ensure a message wakes a parked process; an event alone does not prove the work succeeded. Recovery and verification have to compose across the seams. We will return to four failure questions: what if an agent is wrong, dies, retries or arrives late?

slides.title: The same pieces can travel
slides.caption: Local customization → versioned publication → installation in another workspace
slides.notes: Cupboard makes extensibility part of the architecture. Show the local workspace boundary and the published shelf. Local use does not imply publication. Publication and installation do not imply activation or blanket trust. Different kinds have different review policies; do not say that everything is reviewed. Save package details for the third pass. The public page’s coming-soon markers remain authoritative for the flows it labels.

slides.title: Learn the vocabulary on its own
slides.notes: Make the transition explicit: no system-placement diagrams during this pass. These are independent contract cards. Several are distributable through Cupboard; others are internal coordination primitives. A package kind is not necessarily a running process or a service.

slides.title: Capabilities and structured data

cards.name: Tool
cards.meaning: One action with typed input, guidance and authority.
cards.example: Read an invoice or claim an item.
cards.invariant: A discoverable contract defines the call.

cards.name: Plugin
cards.meaning: A code package that extends the runtime.
cards.example: An integration supplies tools and event families.
cards.invariant: A manifest declares provisions and capabilities.

cards.name: Datatype
cards.meaning: A schema and lifecycle for a structured kind.
cards.example: An installed type defines the shape of a work record.
cards.invariant: Writers and readers share the same shape.

slides.notes: A tool is the capability seam; a plugin is one way to distribute runtime code; a datatype defines structured records. They are different axes. Explain guidance versus validation versus authorization: prose helps choose the right tool, schemas constrain its shape, and guards/authority constrain execution. Use abbreviated contracts, not a full namespace inventory. Show a source excerpt only if someone wants to inspect the seam.

slides.title: Identity and policy

cards.name: Blueprint and identity
cards.example: Extend a parent identity for a project role.
cards.invariant: Canonical layers produce the client render.

cards.name: Mode
cards.meaning: Registered operating posture with an authority boundary.
cards.invariant: State and authority are distinct from prompt prose.

cards.name: Guard
cards.meaning: A policy checked before a matching action.
cards.invariant: Installing a rule and activating it are separate.

slides.notes: Keep identity, blueprint and mode related without making them synonyms. Blueprints are composable definitions; a named identity is the role a session wears; a mode has registry state and a definition. Guard enforcement is more than an instruction to behave. The Cupboard example says an identity pins the installed guard before sessions wearing that identity apply it. A regular-expression guard is a teaching example, not a complete shell-language security boundary.

slides.title: Signals, reactions and time

cards.name: Event and wait
cards.meaning: A named transition and a subscription to it.
cards.example: An item completes; a parked session resumes.
cards.invariant: The key, payload and delivery semantics matter.

cards.name: Reaction rule
cards.meaning: When a condition matches, invoke an action.
cards.example: A successful claim produces coordination output.

cards.name: Routine and action
cards.meaning: A schedule declares when; an action defines what.
cards.example: A recurring sweep starts its named behavior.
cards.invariant: Durable and in-process timers have different lifetimes.

slides.notes: An event declaration is a vocabulary contract, emission is a transition signal, and a wait consumes a signal. A coordination gate can be declared first and latched for late joiners; do not extend that guarantee to every arbitrary event stream. A reaction is a separate edge from a tool call; a guard is a pre-call refusal. Routines separate time policy from executable behavior. Durable reaction delivery is at least once, so retries must be safe; never promise exactly-once effects.

slides.title: Work and coordination

cards.name: Goal, plan and work item
cards.meaning: Outcome → requirements and dependencies → accountable unit.
cards.example: A plan item becomes claimable work.
cards.invariant: Completion needs evidence and a disposition.

cards.name: Scheduler and claim
cards.meaning: Admit eligible work and atomically give it an owner.
cards.example: Pull the next item matching a claim specification.
cards.invariant: Two workers must not both win the same claim.

cards.name: Lock, presence and handoff
cards.meaning: Arbitrate writes, describe liveness and deliver the next action.
cards.example: A blocked write names its current holder.
cards.invariant: A claim is not a file lock; queued delivery is not pickup.

slides.notes: A fleet is a leader/member work topology over these contracts. The leader deals with dependencies, stuck lanes and cross-lane decisions; members pull eligible work. Presence needs more than a heartbeat: live, parked and ended have different delivery consequences. A directed handoff needs a wake and evidence of pickup. File locks serialize actual edits; they are narrower than claiming an entire work item.

slides.title: Live truth and durable continuity

cards.name: State cell
cards.meaning: A registered live value with provenance and unknown states.
cards.example: Read the current holder’s goal at decision time.
cards.invariant: Unread or unknown never means false.

cards.name: Memory, facts and sources
cards.meaning: Recall by meaning; deterministic standing facts; searchable transcripts/docs.
cards.example: A required rule is injected; background knowledge is recalled.

cards.name: Checkpoint and carry
cards.meaning: Persist progress and reconstruct the next session’s working context.
cards.example: Resume the item after a process exits.
cards.invariant: Recover from durable evidence, not an invented summary.

slides.notes: Do not collapse all durable information into ‘memory’. A checkpoint is in-flight work state, a fact is an explicitly standing conclusion with a lifetime, a transcript is a record of what was said, and semantic recall is selective retrieval. The carry inventory assembles identity, modes, held work, context and references for continuity; it does not make recovered prose inherently authoritative. Preserve owner-versus-machine provenance.

slides.title: Reuse and evaluation

cards.name: Recipe
cards.example: Capture a useful real tool run for replay.
cards.invariant: Inspect parameters and side effects before reuse.

cards.name: Rubric and scorecard
cards.meaning: Criteria and method; then an evidence-backed assessment.
cards.example: Judge work against the plan’s actual acceptance bars.
cards.invariant: Self-asserted success does not replace independent judgment.

cards.name: Template, app and theme
cards.meaning: A starting composition, a delivered application, and its visual tokens.
cards.example: Create an app from a maintained template.
cards.invariant: Distribution, execution and visual customization are distinct.

slides.notes: Plans and goals can also be shared as reusable packages, with live execution state kept separate from the template. A recipe reduces repeated orchestration. A rubric makes the method and falsifier explicit; a scorecard records the result. A template helps new apps reuse maintained structure. The appendix holds the complete vocabulary and the corresponding public-page sections.

slides.title: Put the contracts back in the machine
slides.caption: Follow one prepared work item. At every seam: wrong, dead, retried, or late?
slides.notes: This is the same map as pass one. We now attach vocabulary to responsibility and follow causality. The walkthrough is an illustrated scenario; it does not mutate a live workspace. The optional live operator read is secondary evidence, not a dependency of the talk.

slides.title: 1  Claim work, then execute a guarded action
steps: Plan dependencies admit the item
Scheduler atomically assigns the claim
Identity and policy constrain the tool call
Lock arbitration precedes the actual edit
slides.question: If two workers arrive together, who wins—and where is that recorded?
slides.notes: Point to agent fleets, tool fabric, substrate and shared tree in that order. A claim makes ownership visible; file locks guard the write. A failed guard should leave an explicit refusal rather than letting prose override authority. The arrows describe the control path, not a distributed transaction across every component. The current scheduler can atomically claim and declare intent; do not imply all downstream actions are atomic with it.

slides.title: 2  State changes cause reactions and wakes
steps: A successful transition records authoritative state
The declared event carries a structured signal
A reaction invokes its next action
A waiter resumes with the relevant payload
slides.question: A retry must be safe. A late waiter needs the gate’s declared semantics.
slides.notes: Point to the substrate, tool fabric and agents. Distinguish work completion from notification delivery. In the runtime guide, a successful claim causes coordination emission through a lifecycle rule. For a latched coordination gate, a late waiter gets already_fired; do not claim that every event replays history. At-least-once delivery requires a stable deduplication key or idempotent effect. A timer timeout is evidence to investigate the producer, not evidence that it completed.

slides.title: 3  Lose a session without losing the work
steps: Progress and next action are checkpointed
Process/session lifecycle identifies the loss
A successor reorients on durable ownership and evidence
Carry, facts and decisions restore the required context
slides.question: Which state is durable—and which context must be reconstructed?
slides.notes: Point to agent processes, substrate and context/memory. Explain what dies: the OS process and its private context. Explain what should survive: the item, decisions, checkpoints, claims/lifecycle records and verified evidence. A successor still has to check authoritative state; it must not assume a prior shell command succeeded because a note says so. Claims and lock expiry/reconciliation are lifecycle mechanisms rather than magic crash-proof leases. Do not generalize this illustrative flow into a measured recovery SLA.

slides.title: 4  Turn a completion claim into releasable evidence
steps: Work closes with verification evidence
Plan acceptance compares the work with its promised bars
Git automation commits staging; a green verdict promotes main
Deployment ships the green artifact and records its identity
slides.question: ‘The test passed’, ‘the gate is green’, and ‘the fix shipped’ are different claims.
slides.notes: Follow the shared tree through the green gate to production. Plan acceptance and the release gate are distinct checks: the first addresses promised outcomes, the second judges a candidate build. The shared pipeline is asynchronous. A code edit does not instantly appear in the deployed application; final evidence must name the shipped artifact. Explain shared release coupling as a tradeoff, including ownership for red-gate recovery. This slide describes the development release pipeline, not a promise that every output must deploy a service.

slides.title: 5  Make the policy reusable
steps: Author and validate a guard package locally
Publish a public repo revision pinned to a commit
Complete the kind’s review and install the listed revision
An identity pins the guard; matching calls are checked
slides.question: Installation supplies the piece. Activation gives it a role in execution.
slides.notes: Use the Cupboard rule example. A rule folder contains rule.json and listing.json. The page’s current example blocks a force-push through a pre-tool guard. It is a bounded contract example, not a complete sandbox. Publish and review are a separate lifecycle from local execution. A new revision goes through the publication path; a previously approved version keeps serving while its successor waits. Rules and events are packages today, but asking the agent to author them is still marked coming soon on this page. Review differs by kind: the page lists tools/plugins/themes/templates immediately, while reviewed kinds wait. Pinning provides reproducibility; it does not prove code safe.

slides.title: The engineering costs remain visible

columns.title: Explicit machinery
columns.text: Rows, leases, wakes, modes and gates make work inspectable.
columns.cost: They also create more states and recovery paths to test.

columns.title: Composable authority
columns.text: Typed seams and installed policies constrain action.
columns.cost: A reviewed package or a prompt is not a universal security proof.

columns.title: Measured reliability
columns.text: Evidence, falsifiers and distinct release identities narrow claims.
columns.cost: Every detector and verifier can itself be wrong.

slides.notes: Invite technical disagreement. Which invariant would the audience choose to attack first? What state could drift? Where could backpressure accumulate? What if the host or database is down? The architecture makes those questions addressable; it does not eliminate them. Avoid unverified fleet-size, performance, reliability or cost claims. The static pages describe development-source mechanisms and cannot certify the currently installed release.

slides.title: Follow the state, authority and evidence
slides.lead: Three questions for any path through the system
slides.notes: Close with the same system model. Offer the two map references and appendix as the path for deeper questions. The intended takeaway is a causal model of the design, not recall of tool names. Prepared spoken time is 30 minutes; a real presenter should rehearse and decide whether to reserve a longer discussion slot.

slides.title: Discussion routes
slides.notes: This appendix is outside the 30-minute core. Use overview to jump to a question, then return to the core closing slide.

slides.title: Capabilities and composition vocabulary
terms: Typed callable capability with guidance and authority.
Discovery, dispatch and delivery around the client interface.
Runtime extension and its connection to an external service.
Structured kind with schema and lifecycle.
Composable definition and named agent role.
Maintained starting composition and delivered application.
Versioned distribution shelf with kind-specific policy.
slides.notes: These are explanatory definitions, not a one-to-one service inventory. The source pages and current schemas settle exact behavior.

slides.title: Work and coordination vocabulary
terms: Accountable work unit with lifecycle and evidence.
Eligibility and priority for atomic work pulls.
Current ownership of a work unit.
Exclusive arbitration for an actual write.
Leader/member topology over a plan and work queue.
Liveness verdict used to select delivery behavior.
Transfer responsibility and invoke the recipient’s next turn.
Opt into a peer’s relevant working state.
Evaluation method and its evidence-backed result.
slides.notes: Use the claim-versus-lock example when these are confused. A queue entry, a wake receipt and real progress are different observations.

slides.title: Control flow and continuity vocabulary
terms: Define a signal contract; then produce a transition signal.
Register interest with explicit payload and timeout semantics.
Named completion rendezvous; declared coordination gates can latch.
Trigger a following action; or constrain a call before execution.
When behavior runs and what behavior does.
Registered live value with provenance and unknown handling.
Meaning-based recall and deterministic standing context.
Recorded conversation and maintained explanatory source.
Persist work progress and assemble successor context.
Finished owner-facing content with a durable reader.
An explicit peer sharing boundary beyond the local machine.
Outcome acceptance, candidate verdict and shipment identity.
slides.notes: State, signal and context are different kinds of information. Do not imply every event is durable, every field is replicated, or every fact is permanent.
